Myofascial pain

A meta-analysis of upper-trapezius studies reported lower pain and higher pressure-pain thresholds, with low-to-medium certainty. In a recent 52-person sham-controlled trial, 808-nm laser did not outperform sham for pain or trigger-point outcomes; cervical function improved within the active group.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A meta-analysis of upper-trapezius studies reported lower pain and higher pressure-pain thresholds, with low-to-medium certainty. In a recent 52-person sham-controlled trial, 808-nm laser did not outperform sham for pain or trigger-point outcomes; cervical function improved within the active group.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Pain > Myofascial category contains 34 titles: 32 human publications, one systematic review with meta-analysis, and one rabbit experiment. The pooled review reuses primary trials and adds no new cohort. Human studies include 24 randomized trials and eight other clinical reports, with some trials combining PBM with dry needling, exercise, medication, or high-intensity laser.

Human and clinical evidence

The review of upper-trapezius myofascial pain included 17 studies and 944 participants. It reported a medium pooled pain effect for PBM alone and a larger effect when exercise was added, but rated the evidence low to medium and noted protocol variation (Alayat et al. 2022). Individual trials do not all agree. In a recent sham-controlled, double-blind trial of 52 adults with chronic trapezius trigger-point pain, 808-nm laser at 16 J per point did not outperform sham for pain, trigger-point count, or perceived global effect. Cervical function improved within the active group, but that does not establish a between-group pain benefit (do Nascimento Silva et al. 2026). Some combined-treatment trials report pain reduction, but their co-interventions limit attribution (Dalpiaz et al. 2021).

Animal evidence

One rabbit trigger-point experiment measured pain-related biochemical outcomes after laser treatment. It is not clinical evidence and should remain separate from patient pain scores.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo myofascial-pain study is listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Human protocols differ in body site, 808-nm or other laser wavelengths, energy per trigger point, sham design, and added exercise or dry needling. Wavelength is the light's color band and affects tissue penetration. Results from high-intensity devices or laser acupuncture should not automatically be combined with low-level local PBM.

Interpretation

Some pooled and individual studies favor PBM, while a recent rigorous trial found no pain advantage over sham. The evidence supports further protocol-specific testing rather than a single conclusion for all myofascial pain. Larger trials should report clinically meaningful pain and function outcomes separately.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term pain reduction in some upper-trapezius myofascial protocols Low for superiority over sham across patients and protocols, with function evidence less certain
Publications and records34 unique titles (exact Pain > Myofascial)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A meta-analysis found pooled pain and pressure-threshold effects, but included studies were heterogeneous and often small. A recent double-blind trial found no pain advantage over sham, although cervical function improved within the active group. Larger preregistered trials should separate site, dose, and co-interventions.
